subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: Meeting the Funny Man: First Reading Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.59): quick pair-share — things and people that make you laugh.

time_bands.activity: Invite students to look around and think of things or people that make them laugh. In pairs they share one reason each; two or three pairs report to the class to warm up the humorous register of the poem.

Teacher reads the poem aloud with expression, modelling the narrator's baffled tone and the funny man's polite absurdity; students follow in their textbooks (pp. 59–60). Read a second time, inviting students to whisper-read along, attending to the rhyme and rhythm.

Students identify what makes each stanza funny — what the man does, what he says, and how the narrator reacts — sharing observations in an unhurried whole-class discussion. Teacher annotates responses on the board using the students' own words.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's humour rests on sustained inversion — shoe on head, hats on feet, a currant bun offered as a rose — so the opening discussion of real-world funny things helps students recognise the absurdist tradition before they name it. Students often miss the synesthetic oxymorons ('funny sounding sight'); draw attention to these during the second read-aloud. For enrichment, the poem 'My Lost Pencil' on p.69 is available as independent reading pleasure with no formal task attached.
materials: Textbook pp. 59–60 (poem text and pre-reading bubbles activity)

periods.activity_title: True, False and Word Clues: Close Reading the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.61): identify the true statements — pair work, whole-class check.
Let us discuss (p.61): identify 'currant' and 'staggered' from given letter clues.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.61): choose the correct word from brackets for three literary-device questions.

time_bands.activity: Students open to p.61. Teacher re-reads stanzas 1–2 aloud so the facts are fresh before the pair-check task.

Working in pairs, students mark each of the six statements on p.61 as true or false, then justify their choice with a line from the poem. Pairs compare verdicts and the class settles disagreements together.

Teacher presents the letter-frame word clues (C__R____T and S__GG___D) on the board; students race to complete them using context from the poem. Brief discussion of what 'currant' and 'staggered' add to the humour of their stanzas.

periods.teacher_notes: Statement 5 ('the funny man gave a rose') is the richest discussion point: the man offers a currant bun while announcing a rose — students need to distinguish intention from reality. The word-clue activity reinforces vocabulary directly from the poem_text and rewards re-reading. The homework on literary-device identification (bracket choices, p.61) prepares students for the next analytical discussion.
materials: Board or chart for letter-frame display

periods.activity_title: Tone, Rhyme and Synesthetic Phrases: Literary Analysis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.61): complete sentences — tone, rhyme scheme, effect of 'funny' repetition.
Let us discuss (p.61–62): rewrite inverted line; explain synesthetic phrases 'funny sounding sight' and 'funny feeling sound'.

time_bands.activity: Students complete the three sentence-frames on p.61 (tone, rhyme scheme, effect of 'funny' repetition) independently, then share with a partner. Teacher facilitates whole-class convergence, drawing out the ABCB pattern and the 'bouncy, song-like quality' the rhyme creates.

Teacher writes the inverted lines 'But never had I seen before / Such a funny sounding sight' on the board. Students rewrite them in normal word order and compare, noticing how the inversion adds a dramatic pause. Class then unpacks the synesthetic phrases — 'funny sounding sight' (a sound that is a sight) and 'funny feeling sound' (a sound that is a feeling) — as examples of the poem's playful cross-sensory language.

Brief review of the homework bracket-choice answers (alliteration, dialogue vs. monologue, humorous scene) from p.61; teacher clarifies the difference between alliteration and other devices using the poem's own phrases 'sounding sight' and 'hopped home'. Students record corrected answers.

periods.teacher_notes: The synesthetic oxymorons ('funny sounding sight', 'funny feeling sound', 'funny looking smell') are the poem's most distinctive literary move; spending unhurried time here is productive. Students often initially label 'funny sounding sight' as a metaphor — redirect them by asking which two senses are being mixed. The ABCB rhyme scheme may be new terminology; mapping it stanza-by-stanza on the board helps.
materials: Textbook pp. 61–62 (Let us discuss and Let us think tasks)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.62): extract 1 — 'Allow me to present…', four sub-questions.
Let us think and reflect (p.63): extract 2 — 'You never heard…hopped home on his head', four sub-questions.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.63): five reflective questions — character trait, mood, alternative title, dialogues, poet's message.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 1 (p.62) aloud: the man addresses the narrator as 'Your Highness', offers a currant bun as a rose, and the narrator staggers back. Students work individually on the four sub-questions — why 'Your Highness', the polite-request phrase, what 'staggered' expresses — then pairs compare before class discussion.

Teacher reads Extract 2 (p.63) aloud: the narrator calls the man 'my friend' and asks about the hats; the man hops home on his head. Students tackle the four sub-questions — which line shows a unique sound, why the narrator uses 'my friend', what the man's non-answer reveals, how the last line makes readers feel — sharing in a whole-class discussion that focuses on the poem's permanent upside-down ending.

periods.teacher_notes: The address 'Your Highness' is humorous precisely because it is over-formal from an upside-down stranger; students may need prompting to see this as part of the man's impeccable-yet-absurd courtesy. The homework set of five reflective questions (p.63) covers the larger evaluative and creative moves — character trait, mood, alternative title, dialogue purpose, poet's message — and prepares rich material for speaking activities.
materials: Textbook pp. 62–63 (Let us think and reflect, extracts 1 and 2)

periods.activity_title: Listening to a Personal Funny Incident: Sequencing Events

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.65): listen and select the picture related to the narration.
Let us listen (p.66): second listen — arrange seven events in order of occurrence.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the listening task: a girl narrates a funny personal incident about muddling up shoes and a plate while distracted. Students look at the four pictures on p.65 and predict which will match the story.

Teacher reads the transcript aloud at natural pace (p.88). Students listen and circle the picture on p.65 that best relates to the narration; pairs compare choices, then the class settles on the answer.
Brief pause; students read the seven events on p.66 silently to prepare for the second listen.

Teacher reads the transcript a second time. Students number the seven events in the order they hear them. Pairs compare their sequences, resolve any differences, and the class constructs the correct order together on the board.
Quick reflective share: ask students to name something from their own life they have done absent-mindedly, connecting the listening text's humour to the poem's comic spirit.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript (p.88) describes a girl who, while preoccupied with exam preparation, places her shoes in the kitchen and her plate on her desk. The comic confusion echoes the funny man's upside-down logic and links listening to the poem's theme of things in the wrong place. Students frequently confuse the order of 'removed shoes' and 'prepared for presentation' — listen carefully for the temporal markers 'after a long day' and 'I removed my shoes at the door'.
materials: Transcript text (p.88) read aloud by teacher

periods.activity_title: Telling Jokes with Voice: Paired Performance

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.66): read and perform the man-and-God joke in pairs with correct character voices.
Let us speak (p.66): create and perform an original joke in pairs before the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the man-and-God joke on p.66 once, modelling the three voices: narrator (matter-of-fact), man (louder, respectful), God (deep, pleasant). Students note the voice shifts and discuss why each voice fits the character.
In pairs, students take turns playing narrator, man, and God, performing the joke from p.66. Teacher circulates, nudging pairs to commit to the voice distinctions rather than reading in a flat tone.

Pairs spend time creating their own short joke — two to three exchanges — and rehearsing it with clear character voices. Teacher reminds them of the punchline structure: set-up, build, unexpected twist.
Two or three volunteer pairs perform their original jokes for the class. Audience listens and identifies what made each punchline funny.

periods.teacher_notes: The joke's humour hinges on the double meaning of 'a minute' — encourage students to identify this before they perform so the punchline lands. Students who are hesitant to perform before the class may begin with a whisper rehearsal; the constitution of the poem's narrator — baffled but friendly — can be a useful model for their own performance confidence. Remind the class that good joke-telling is about timing, not volume.
materials: Textbook p.66 (Let us speak — man-and-God joke and creation task)

periods.activity_title: Writing a Limerick: Structure, Draft and Share

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.66–67): identify limerick rhyme scheme from examples, then write own limerick using AABBA template.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the two example limericks on p.66–67 aloud with exaggerated bounce. Students map the rhyme scheme (AABBA) by marking end-sounds, then explain in one sentence why the short lines create a comic effect.

Teacher walks through the template on p.67 line by line: Line 1 introduces a person or place, Lines 2–3 share the silly story (long lines, A rhyme), Line 4 adds a detail (short, B rhyme), Line 5 delivers the unexpected ending (long, A rhyme). Students choose their own subject and draft a limerick, consulting the template.
Pairs swap limericks, check the AABBA pattern and highlight any line that breaks the scheme. Writers revise based on the feedback, adjusting syllable count or rhyme as needed.
Three or four students read their final limericks aloud to the class; the class claps on the punchy last line. Teacher praises inventive rhymes and comic twists.

periods.teacher_notes: The limerick is a contained, self-revising writing task — drafting, peer feedback and revision all fit within this sitting. Students often struggle most with the short fourth line (B rhyme); suggest they write line 4 before line 3 to get the B rhyme settled first. The unexpected ending (Line 5) is the payoff — encourage students to think of their funniest idea and save it for last.
materials: Textbook pp. 66–67 (Let us write — example limericks and template)
Lined paper or notebooks for drafting

periods.activity_title: Phrasal Verbs with 'Take': Meaning, Form and Use

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.64): match five 'take' phrasal verbs to their meanings in Column 2.
Let us learn (p.64): fill five blanks using take up/after/in/over/off with correct tense.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.65): arrange movement words (sprint, trot, jog) by pace and write five phrasal-verb sentences.

time_bands.activity: Teacher highlights the three phrasal verbs from the poem — 'walking down', 'taking out', 'sat down' — on the board, noting that each verb combines with a particle to create a meaning different from the verb alone. Students predict one meaning before turning to p.64.

Students work individually to match the five 'take' phrasal verbs on p.64 (take up, take after, take in, take over, take off) to their meanings in Column 2. Pairs compare; teacher confirms answers and asks students to illustrate each meaning with a brief example sentence.

Students complete the five-blank fill-in task on p.64, choosing the correct phrasal verb and adjusting tense where needed. Teacher circulates and addresses tense-change questions; the class checks answers together, noting why tense shifts in items 4 and 5.

Introduce the homework task (p.65): arrange sprint, trot and jog on the pace scale and write five original phrasal-verb sentences. Teacher clarifies the scale's anchors (stagger → walk → … → run) so students can attempt it confidently.

periods.teacher_notes: Phrasal verbs with 'take' are highly productive in spoken and written English; the poem's own 'taking out' is the best entry point for contextual prediction. Students frequently confuse 'take in' (comprehend) with 'take over' (assume control); contrasting the two with brief scenarios resolves this quickly. The movement-word scale in the homework links directly to the poem's vocabulary of walking, staggering and hopping.
materials: Textbook p.64 (Let us learn — match and fill-in tasks)

periods.activity_title: Building Phrasal Verbs: Look, Run, Put, Break, Call

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.64): match look/run/put/break/call with particles; write meanings in Column 3.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the five base verbs (look, run, put, break, call) and the ten particles (after, away, up, for, in, on, into, down, off, out) on the board. Students brainstorm in groups of three: which combinations feel natural and what might they mean?

Students work through the task on p.64, pairing each base verb with at least two particles and writing the resulting phrasal verb plus a brief meaning in Column 3. Teacher circulates, prompting students to check their combinations by using them in a short spoken sentence.

Groups share their best or most surprising combinations with the class; teacher builds a class list on the board. Special attention to pairs where the same particle changes the meaning dramatically (e.g., 'put on' versus 'put down').
Quick consolidation: teacher draws attention to the pace-scale homework responses (stagger → walk → trot → hop → jog → run → sprint), confirming the movement continuum from the poem's vocabulary.

periods.teacher_notes: The open-ended nature of this task — multiple valid combinations per verb — encourages productive group experimentation rather than a single right answer. Students may form combinations that are not standard British or Indian English; accept and discuss them as a linguistic curiosity. The connection between the poem's 'hopped' and the pace-scale consolidation at the end rewards students who noticed the poem's movement vocabulary.
materials: Textbook p.64 (Let us learn — verb-plus-particle matching task)

periods.activity_title: Wit Across Cultures: Sharing Humorous Stories and Poems

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.67): read and share a story featuring Tenali Rama, Birbal, Mullah Nasruddin or Vikramaditya-Betal.
Let us explore (p.68): share a humorous or nonsense poem from a native language similar in style to 'A Funny Man'.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the four wit-and-wisdom figures from ancient Indian literature listed on p.67 — Tenali Rama, Birbal, Mullah Nasruddin, King Vikramaditya and Betal — with a quick one-sentence description of each character's hallmark style.

Students who have read a story featuring one of these characters share a brief retelling (one to two minutes each); two or three students present, and the class discusses what made each figure's humour clever or moral. Teacher connects the characters' wit to the funny man's upside-down logic.

Students share a humorous or nonsense poem from their native language, explaining what makes it funny — rhythm, inversion, wordplay, absurdity. Teacher draws brief comparisons with Natalie Joan's poem and mentions Sukumar Ray's 'Abol Tabol' as a parallel Indian nonsense tradition.
Brief closing reflection: each student names in one word what humour in literature gives a reader. Teacher collects the words on the board as a final thought cloud for the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have not had access to a library before this sitting should still be able to participate — the task invites a story or poem they already know, not one they were required to find after a previous sitting. If a student cannot share a native-language poem, encourage them to describe a funny scene from a film or television programme and identify the comic device. The Sukumar Ray reference on p.68 is a rich extension for curious students.
materials: Optional: printed short excerpt from Abol Tabol or a Birbal/Tenali Rama story for students without prior access

items.source_lo: Student analyses a nonsense poem's comic devices, tone, and structural features using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Absurdist inversion, synesthetic oxymorons, ABCB rhyme scheme, Natalie Joan's funny man character.
items.item_stem: Read the lines from 'A Funny Man' beginning 'He wore a shoe upon his head / And hats upon his feet.' Which of the following best describes what the poet achieves by dressing the funny man this way?

options.label: A
options.text: She shows that the funny man is too poor to afford proper clothing.

options.label: B
options.text: She establishes the poem's comic tone through physical inversion of everyday objects.

options.label: C
options.text: She suggests the funny man is preparing for a fancy-dress competition.

options.label: D
options.text: She reveals that the funny man lives in an unusually cold place.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student read the inversion as realistic poverty rather than deliberate absurdist comedy.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates a literal reading of costume without recognising the poem's sustained comic logic.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Shows the student supplied an external explanation where none exists in the poem.

items.source_lo: Student analyses a nonsense poem's comic devices, tone, and structural features using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Absurdist inversion, synesthetic oxymorons, ABCB rhyme scheme, Natalie Joan's funny man character.
items.item_stem: In 'A Funny Man', the narrator describes experiencing 'a funny sounding sight' and 'a funny feeling sound'. What does Natalie Joan achieve by combining words from different senses in these phrases, and how does this contribute to the overall tone of the poem?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The phrases mix sense words — sight with sound, and feeling with sound — to create synesthetic oxymorons that reflect the funny man's upside-down world. This cross-sensory language heightens the poem's gleefully comic and surreal tone, signalling that normal logic does not apply in the funny man's presence.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a personal anecdote and demonstrates comprehension by selecting relevant information and sequencing events using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Girl's distracted kitchen-and-shoes mix-up incident; seven events to sequence; comic absent-mindedness.
items.item_stem: Listen to the girl's account of what happened after she returned home from studying. Which of the following statements correctly describes what she did when she first entered her home?

options.label: A
options.text: She went straight to the kitchen and served herself lunch.

options.label: B
options.text: She removed her shoes at the door and went to the kitchen.

options.label: C
options.text: She placed her plate on her desk before eating.

options.label: D
options.text: She laughed at herself and put her shoes in the kitchen.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Conflates the first and second actions — removing shoes happened before going to the kitchen.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Describes an action from the middle of the story, not the first thing she did on entering.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Captures an action from the end of the story and misplaces it at the beginning.

items.source_context: Girl's distracted kitchen-and-shoes mix-up incident; seven events to sequence; comic absent-mindedness.
items.item_stem: In the girl's narration about her absent-minded day, she mixed up where she put two objects. Complete the table below with the correct locations, based on what you heard.
items.visual_stimulus:
Object|Where she placed it by mistake|Where it should have gone
Her plate|_______|_______
Her shoes|_______|_______

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Her plate — placed by mistake on her desk; should have gone in the kitchen. 2. Her shoes — placed by mistake in the kitchen; should have gone in her room.

items.item_stem: With a partner, perform a short two-character humorous dialogue in which one character misunderstands the other because of a double meaning in a word or phrase. Each partner plays one character. Use a clearly different voice for each character.

expected_elements: Uses a noticeably distinct voice or tone for each character.
The dialogue includes a word or phrase with a double meaning.
The misunderstanding leads to a clear, funny punchline.
Speaks audibly and at a pace the audience can follow.

items.item_stem: Imagine you meet a character as absurd as the funny man from Natalie Joan's poem — someone whose behaviour is the opposite of what you expect. Tell your class about this meeting. Share your opinion of what the character's behaviour reveals about how humour works, giving at least one reason for your view.

expected_elements: Describes a specific absurd behaviour that inverts normal expectation.
States a clear personal opinion about what the humour reveals.
Supports the opinion with at least one reason or example.
Speaks in a lively register appropriate to a comic account.

items.item_stem: Write a limerick of exactly five lines about the funny man or any character who behaves in a topsy-turvy way. Your limerick must follow the AABBA rhyme scheme: Lines 1, 2 and 5 rhyme with each other (A), and Lines 3 and 4 rhyme with each other (B). Line 1 introduces your character; Lines 2–4 tell a silly story; Line 5 gives an unexpected ending.

expected_elements: Five lines present; AABBA rhyme scheme correctly applied.
Line 1 introduces a character or place clearly.
Lines 3–4 are noticeably shorter, matching limerick rhythm.
Line 5 delivers a comic or unexpected twist ending.

items.source_context: Limerick form, AABBA rhyme scheme, five-line structure — introduction, silly story, unexpected ending.
items.item_stem: The funny man in Natalie Joan's poem lives in a world where everything is upside-down. Write a short paragraph (five to seven sentences) from the funny man's point of view, explaining why he thinks the narrator is the one who is confused. Use imaginative detail and make your writing playful in tone.

expected_elements: Written from the funny man's first-person perspective throughout.
Inverts the narrator's perspective — treats the narrator as the odd one.
Uses playful, comic language consistent with the poem's absurdist tone.
Includes at least one specific detail from the poem (shoe, hats, currant bun, or hopping).

items.item_stem: Match each phrasal verb in Column A with its correct meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A|Column B
take after|to assume control or responsibility
take in|to begin practising or studying something
take off|to resemble a family member
take over|to become quickly popular or successful
take up|to understand or comprehend something

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1-c, 2-e, 3-d, 4-a, 5-b (take after–resemble a family member; take in–comprehend; take off–become popular quickly; take over–assume control; take up–begin studying/practising).

answer_key.right: to become quickly popular or successful
to begin practising or studying something

items.item_stem: The funny man in the poem 'took out' a currant bun and 'walked down' the street. Using phrasal verbs formed from the verbs in the box (look, run, put, break, call), write three sentences that describe unusual or funny actions a street performer might do. Each sentence must use a different phrasal verb and show clearly that you understand its meaning.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any three sentences that each use a correctly formed phrasal verb from the set (e.g., 'look after', 'run into', 'put on', 'break out', 'call off') and use it with a meaning consistent with standard usage, applied to a street-performer context.

items.item_stem: Choose one of the classical Indian wit figures mentioned in 'Let us explore' — Tenali Rama, Birbal, Mullah Nasruddin, or Vikramaditya and Betal. Write an account (one paragraph, six to eight sentences) of a story you have read or heard about this figure. Your account must describe the situation the character faced, explain the clever or funny way the character responded, and state what lesson or idea the story conveys.

expected_elements: Names the chosen figure and the story's situation clearly.
Describes the character's clever or humorous response in detail.
States the moral, lesson or deeper idea the story conveys.
Writes six to eight sentences in coherent paragraph form.

items.source_context: Tenali Rama, Birbal, Mullah Nasruddin, Vikramaditya-Betal wit-and-wisdom stories; native-language nonsense poems; Sukumar Ray's Abol Tabol.
items.item_stem: Find a humorous or nonsense poem in your native language or in any Indian language you know. Prepare a short presentation (two to three minutes) for your class in which you: (a) read or recite the poem; (b) explain in English what makes it funny — focusing on the device it uses most (inversion, wordplay, absurdity, rhythm, or another); and (c) compare it in one or two sentences with Natalie Joan's 'A Funny Man', noting one similarity and one difference.

expected_elements: A poem is identified and read or recited to the class.
The dominant comic device is named and explained with an example.
One clear similarity with 'A Funny Man' is stated.
One clear difference from 'A Funny Man' is stated.
